extracted.intended_audience: intellectual property managers, technology transfer professionals, and patent attorneys handling federally funded inventions and/or foreign filings
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for deciding whether, where, when, and how to file patent applications outside the United States and the statutory/contractual requirements that apply to subject inventions arising under federal funding (Bayh‑Dole and agency clauses). Covers reporting, rights allocation, PCT/ national/ regional routes, timelines, and agency procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting on Utilization of Subject Inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: The Contractor agrees to submit on request periodic reports no more frequently than annually on the utilization of a subject invention or on efforts at obtaining such utilization that are being made by the contractor or its licensees or assignees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reports shall include information regarding the status of development, date of first commercial sale or use, gross royalties received by the contractor, and such other data and information as the agency may reasonably specify. Contractor must also provide additional reports as may be requested in connection with any march‑in proceeding. (Also: agency agrees it will not disclose such information outside the government without contractor permission under 35 U.S.C. 202(c)(5).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Non‑disclosure of Contractor Reports (35 U.S.C. 202(c)(5))
rubrics_metrics.description: As required by 35 U.S.C. 202(c)(5), the agency agrees it will not disclose such information to persons outside the government without permission of the contractor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This protects sensitive commercialization and royalty data supplied in utilization reports; contractor permission is required for disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for United States Industry (manufacturing clause)
rubrics_metrics.description: The contractor agrees that neither it nor any assignee will grant to any person the exclusive right to use or sell any subject invention in the United States unless such person agrees that any products embodying the subject invention or produced through the use of the subject invention will be manufactured substantially in the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The requirement may be waived by the Federal agency upon a showing that reasonable but unsuccessful efforts were made to grant licenses on similar terms to potential licensees likely to manufacture substantially in the U.S., or that domestic manufacture is not commercially feasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: March‑in Rights
rubrics_metrics.description: The Federal agency has the right to require the contractor, an assignee or exclusive licensee of a subject invention to grant licenses to responsible applicants, or to grant such licenses itself if necessary, under the procedures in 37 CFR 401.6 and agency regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agency may act if it determines that: (1) contractor/assignee has not taken or is not expected to take effective steps to achieve practical application; (2) action is necessary to alleviate unmet health or safety needs; (3) action is necessary to meet requirements for public use specified by regulation; or (4) the U.S. manufacturing agreement required by paragraph (i) has not been obtained/waived or a licensee is in breach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special Provisions for Nonprofit Organizations — assignment approval
rubrics_metrics.description: If the contractor is a nonprofit organization, rights to a subject invention in the United States may not be assigned without the approval of the Federal agency, except where such assignment is made to an organization which has as one of its primary functions the management of inventions, provided that such assignee will be subject to the same provisions as the contractor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This limits transfers of title by nonprofit contractors and conditions permissible assignees to be subject to the same Bayh‑Dole provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special Provisions for Nonprofit Organizations — royalty sharing with inventors
rubrics_metrics.description: The contractor will share royalties collected on a subject invention with the inventor, including Federal employee co‑inventors (when the agency deems it appropriate) when the subject invention is assigned in accordance with 35 U.S.C. 202(e) and 37 CFR 401.10.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires nonprofit contractors to provide inventor compensation/royalty sharing upon assignment as specified by statute/regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special Provisions for Nonprofit Organizations — use of royalties
rubrics_metrics.description: The balance of any royalties or income earned by the contractor with respect to subject inventions, after payment of expenses (including payments to inventors) incidental to the administration of subject inventions, will be utilized for the support of scientific research or education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Net income from subject inventions must be reinvested into research/education activities rather than for unrelated commercial purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special Provisions for Nonprofit Organizations — preference for small business licensees
rubrics_metrics.description: The contractor will make efforts that are reasonable under the circumstances to attract licensees of subject inventions that are small business firms and will give a preference to a small business firm when licensing a subject invention if the small business firm has a plan equally likely to bring the invention to practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contractor must be satisfied that the small business has capability/resources. Secretary may review the contractor’s licensing program and require negotiated changes if reasonable steps to implement this paragraph are not being taken.

rubrics_metrics.name: DOE‑Specific Modifications for Nonprofit DOE Facility Operators
rubrics_metrics.description: When DOE uses alternative provisions under §401.3(a)(4), the clause is modified for nonprofit DOE facility operators, including special rules for inventions occurring under naval nuclear propulsion or weapons‑related programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If invention occurred under such DOE programs the contractor agrees to assign the government the entire right, title, and interest unless a greater‑rights request is submitted and processed per 37 CFR 401.15; contractor (or employee‑inventor) may request greater rights at disclosure or within a reasonable time thereafter; contractor must submit a written statement within 90 days whether the invention occurred under such programs or the assign‑all subparagraph will apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allocation of Principal Rights (contractor retention and government license)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Contractor may retain the entire right, title, and interest throughout the world to each subject invention subject to the provisions of this clause, and 35 U.S.C. 203. With respect to any subject invention in which the Contractor retains title, the Federal Government shall have a nonexclusive, nontransferable, irrevocable, paid‑up license to practice or have practiced for or on behalf of the United States the subject invention throughout the world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sets the default ownership allocation and the government's retained license when contractor keeps title.

rubrics_metrics.name: CRADA‑Related Rights and Option to Collaborators
rubrics_metrics.description: If the Contractor performs services at a Government owned and operated laboratory or at a Government owned and contractor operated laboratory directed by the Government to fulfill the Government’s obligations under a CRADA, the Government may require the Contractor to negotiate an agreement with the CRADA collaborating party or parties regarding allocation of rights to any subject invention the Contractor makes under the CRADA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agreement should be negotiated prior to undertaking the CRADA work or, with permission, upon identification of a subject invention. In absence of such agreement, the Contractor agrees to grant the collaborating party or parties an option for a license in its inventions of the same scope and terms set forth in the CRADA for inventions made by the Government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deferred Determinations (requests for greater rights)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applies to requests for greater rights where deferred determination provisions were included in the funding agreement; a contractor requesting greater rights should include information on plans and intentions to bring the invention to practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agency should seek to make a determination within 90 days (or sooner if a statutory bar to patenting is imminent). If a bar is imminent, unless the agency plans to file on its own, it shall authorize the contractor to file a patent application pending determination (normally at contractor’s risk and expense). If the agency later refuses to allow the contractor to retain title and elects to proceed under government ownership, it shall reimburse the contractor for preparing and filing costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency Determination Standard when Exception Circumstances Have Changed
rubrics_metrics.description: If the circumstances that led the agency to invoke an exception are not applicable or no longer valid, the agency should allow the contractor to retain title on the same conditions as if the standard clause had been used originally, unless the invention has been licensed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If not applicable, agency shall decide whether its own plans would better promote policies/objectives of 35 U.S.C. 200 than contractor ownership; agency may impose conditions or expanded government license for specific applications rather than take title.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal Rights for Title Determinations
rubrics_metrics.description: A determination not to allow the contractor to retain title to a subject invention or to restrict its title with conditions differing from the standard clause, unless made by the head of the agency, shall be appealable by the contractor to an agency official at a level above the person who made the determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The appeal is subject to the procedures applicable to appeals under §401.11 of this part.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electronic Filing of Required Reports and Elections
rubrics_metrics.description: The written report required in (c)(1) of the standard clause in §401.14(a), the written election required in (c)(2), and the close‑out report and specified information in §401.5 may be electronically filed unless otherwise requested or directed by the agency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permits electronic submission of the statutory/contractual reports and elections to streamline compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing Decision — factors to consider for foreign patent protection
rubrics_metrics.description: Decision whether to pursue patent protection outside the United States should balance commercial and marketing potential internationally, the cost of obtaining and maintaining patent rights in each country, and whether the invention is patentable under applicable foreign patent laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Engage foreign counsel as needed; a general understanding of foreign procedures helps manage prosecution and cost; seek professional legal advice before undertaking a foreign‑filing strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Where to File — business and legal considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Deciding in which countries to pursue protection is often a business decision based on (a) perceived commercial value of the invention in the country and (b) the cost of obtaining patent rights in the country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: file in countries constituting major market share unless prosecuting in multiple countries exceeds budget. Also determine whether subject matter is patentable in the countries considered (e.g., business methods may not be patentable in some jurisdictions).

rubrics_metrics.name: When to File — Paris Convention 12‑month priority window
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally decide whether to pursue patent protection outside the U.S. no later than twelve months from the filing date of your original U.S. patent application (nonprovisional or provisional) to claim priority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If filed within 12 months, most corresponding foreign applications can be filed claiming priority to the original U.S. filing date; priority preserves the earlier effective date for prior‑art purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to File — three international filing routes
rubrics_metrics.description: Three routes: (1) filing separate national applications directly; (2) filing applications in regional patent offices (e.g., EPO, ARIPO, OAPI, Eurasian); and (3) filing an international patent application under the Patent Cooperation Treaty (PCT).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pros/cons: national/regional filings may be quicker but incur individual fees earlier; PCT preserves rights across many countries without immediate national costs and provides international search/examination reports that many national offices use as a starting point.

rubrics_metrics.name: National Filing — prepare application per country requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare and file, with assistance of a foreign patent attorney, an application that meets the requirements prescribed by the patent laws of the country in which you are filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differences from U.S. practice include annual annuity payments for pending/issued cases and options to defer examination for years. Expect office actions similar to USPTO; work with local counsel to manage prosecution and costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regional Filing — designation and registration requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: When filing in a regional patent office (e.g., EPO), upon issuance you may register the patent in member states to obtain rights; you must designate the countries in which you want to register your patent at filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you fail to designate a particular country at filing, you will not be able to register the regional patent in that nation. Understand member states and designation rules for each regional office.

rubrics_metrics.name: PCT Filing — preservation of options and overview of Chapter I/II processes
rubrics_metrics.description: PCT filing provides a single international application convertible into multiple national applications up to 30 (and sometimes 31) months from filing or priority date and includes international search (ISR) and written opinion (ISA‑WO), publication at ~18 months, and optional Chapter II international preliminary examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ISA prepares ISR and ISA‑WO about 16 months from earliest priority date addressing novelty, inventive step, and industrial applicability and may point out form/clarity objections. Article 19 claim amendments may be filed but are not substantively considered during international examination. IPRP (Ch I) issued if no Chapter II; Chapter II (demand filed at later of 22 months or 3 months after ISR) allows dialogue and may produce IPRP (Ch II) ~28 months. National conversion deadlines typically at 30/31 months (extended from 19 months for many states). Many national offices use the international examiner’s decision as a starting point—resolving issues during PCT can reduce national prosecution costs. Confidentiality considerations: selecting EPO vs USPTO as ISA/IPEA can affect public availability of prosecution file.

rubrics_metrics.name: National Conversion Deadlines and Options under the PCT
rubrics_metrics.description: Originally national conversion was at 19 months under Chapter I, but deadlines have been extended to 30 (and in some cases 31) months for national conversion; some countries still require an earlier choice at 19 months.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check each designated state's national law: if a state retains the earlier deadline you may need to convert earlier or use regional conversion options. Chapter II remains optional but may be favorable when the ISA‑WO is negative.

rubrics_metrics.name: PCT Examination Timelines and Documents (ISR, ISA‑WO, publication, IPRP)
rubrics_metrics.description: Approximately 16 months from earliest priority date the ISA will issue an international search report (ISR) and written opinion (ISA‑WO); publication occurs at 18 months (with ISR and any Article 19 amendments); ISA‑WO becomes publicly available after 30 months; IPRP (Ch I) issued if no Chapter II; IPRP (Ch II) issued ~28 months if Chapter II demand filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ISA‑WO gives preliminary opinion on novelty, inventive step, industrial applicability, and form/clarity objections; Article 19 amendments are not substantively considered during international examination; resolving issues during PCT can streamline national prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pros and Cons of Filing Routes
rubrics_metrics.description: National/regional filings may obtain foreign patent rights faster, but require earlier payment of national filing/translation/attorney/annuity fees. PCT preserves international options and delays national costs, while providing search/examination reports many national offices rely on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose route based on budget, timeline, need for early national grants, and desire to preserve options while collecting additional information about value/patentability in different countries.

rubrics_metrics.name: National Examination Process — variability in substantive patentability requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: National examination is typically the most complex and expensive part of obtaining foreign patent rights; many requirements for patentability (e.g., novelty, written description) differ from country to country and may preclude protection in some nations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: U.S. uses relative novelty while Europe and Japan use variations on absolute novelty — understand key differences among jurisdictions and rely on foreign counsel to manage prosecution strategies compatible across jurisdictions.
